t: Maximum Number of Occurrences of a Substring
o: We must find the substring of s that occurs the most times (overlaps allowed), subject to two constraints: it uses at most maxLetters distinct characters and its length lies in [minSize, maxSize]. In example 1, "aab" appears at indices 0 and 6, giving 2. In example 2, "aaa" appears at indices 0 and 1 (overlapping), giving 2. The crucial observation is that we never need to consider lengths greater than minSize: any valid substring of length L > minSize contains a prefix of length minSize that has no more unique characters and occurs at least as many times. So it suffices to count occurrences of every length-minSize window whose distinct character count is ≤ maxLetters.
k: Only substrings of length exactly minSize matter: a longer valid substring always contains a shorter one that is at least as frequent and satisfies the letter constraint.
A sliding window of fixed size minSize lets us maintain distinct-character counts incrementally in O(1) amortized per step.
Overlapping occurrences are allowed, so every starting index contributes an occurrence independently.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Lengths
a.i: For every starting index, try every length from minSize to maxSize, check the number of distinct characters, and tally valid substrings in a hash map. This directly mirrors the problem statement. It works because n ≤ 10^5 but maxSize ≤ 26, so total work is about n * 26 * 26 which is acceptable, though far from optimal.
s: Initialize an empty hash map counting substring frequencies.
For each start index i, for each length len from minSize to maxSize:
Extract s[i..i+len-1] and count its distinct characters.
If distinct characters ≤ maxLetters, increment the counter for that substring.
Return the maximum value in the map (0 if empty).
a.t: O(n * maxSize^2) — for each of ~n starts we try up to 26 lengths, and checking distinct characters costs up to 26.
a.sp: O(n * maxSize) — the hash map may store up to n strings of length up to 26.

a.n: Approach 2: Fixed Sliding Window of Size minSize (Optimal)
a.i: Since any longer valid substring implies an equally-frequent valid prefix of length minSize, we only slide a window of exactly minSize across s. We maintain a frequency array of the 26 letters inside the window to track the distinct count in O(1) per slide, and a hash map from substring to occurrence count. The answer is the maximum count among windows with distinct count ≤ maxLetters.
s: Build the first window s[0..minSize-1], recording letter frequencies and distinct count, then add it to the map if valid.
Slide the window one character at a time: add the incoming letter, remove the outgoing letter, updating the distinct count when a frequency hits 1 or drops to 0.
For each window position, if distinct count ≤ maxLetters, increment the map entry for the current window substring and update the answer.
Return the best count found (0 if none).
a.t: O(n * minSize) — one pass over s with O(1) window updates; hashing/constructing each minSize-length substring costs O(minSize) ≤ O(26).
a.sp: O(n * minSize) — the hash map stores up to n keys of length minSize; the frequency array is O(26).

w: In an interview, lead with the key reduction (only length minSize matters) and present Approach 2; mention Approach 1 briefly as the naive baseline. Common pitfalls: forgetting that occurrences can overlap (no non-overlap requirement), iterating lengths above minSize unnecessarily, and off-by-one errors when the window becomes active (start counting once i ≥ minSize - 1). Edge cases: minSize equal to s.length (single window), no valid substring at all (return 0), and maxLetters ≥ 26 (constraint never binds). Likely follow-ups: can you avoid materializing substrings via rolling hashes (Rabin-Karp) to get true O(n)? What if the alphabet were unbounded? How would you report the substring itself rather than just its count?
